steps.body: Simplifying divides top and bottom by their greatest common factor. The value does not move; the numbers just get smaller.
steps.narration: Simplifying divides top and bottom by their greatest common factor. The value does not move; the numbers just get smaller.

widget.successFeedback: 2/3 — dividing both parts by 4 leaves the same amount in larger pieces.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 2/3 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 2/3 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: That divided only the TOP by 4 and left the bottom alone, which shrinks the amount instead of renaming it.
That SUBTRACTED 4 from both parts. Simplifying divides both by a shared factor; subtracting changes the value.

predict.prompt: Simplifying 8/12 to 2/3, does the amount change?
predict.reveal: Dividing both parts by 4 re-cuts the same length into fewer, larger pieces.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u simplify.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u simplify a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Simplify 4/6 by dividing both by 2. What is the simplified numerator (top)?

commonErrors.feedback: That left the fraction unsimplified — dividing both parts by 2 shrinks the numbers, not the value.
That reported the simplified DENOMINATOR; the question asks for the top.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.
